## What it says
For a separable isogeny $\varphi : E_1 \to E_2$ of elliptic curves over a field $K$, the $\varphi$-descent sequence $E_2(K)/\varphi(E_1(K)) \to \mathrm{Sel}_\varphi \to Ш(E_1)[\varphi]$ is exact at the Selmer group: an element of $\mathrm{Sel}_\varphi$ maps to $0$ in $Ш(E_1)[\varphi]$ exactly when it comes from a point of $E_2(K)$ under the Kummer map.

- `[Field K]`: $K$ is a field; `Field` is the class of fields.
- `[W₁.IsElliptic] [W₂.IsElliptic]`: the Weierstrass curves $W_1$, $W_2$ over $K$ have nonzero discriminant, so they are elliptic curves $E_1$, $E_2$.
- `[(i : ι) → Field (L i)] [(i : ι) → Algebra K (L i)]`: a family of fields $L_i$, indexed by a type $\iota$, each an extension of $K$ (the `Algebra` structure).
- `(φ : Isogeny W₁.toAffine W₂.toAffine)`: a nonzero isogeny `φ` from $E_1$ to $E_2$ defined over $K$.
- `(τ : (i : ι) → SeparableClosure K →ₐ[K] SeparableClosure (L i))`: for each $i$, an embedding `τ` over $K$ of a separable closure of $K$ into one of $L_i$. These give the restriction maps from the Galois cohomology of $K$ to that of each $L_i$, relative to which the Selmer and Shafarevich–Tate groups are defined.
- `[Algebra.IsSeparable (↥φ.fieldPullback.fieldRange) W₁.toAffine.FunctionField]`: the function field of $E_1$ is separable over the pulled-back function field of $E_2$, that is, $\varphi$ is separable.
- `[DecidableEq K]`: equality in $K$ can be decided, which the group law on points uses; a technical hypothesis.
- The conclusion, `Function.Exact ⇑(φ.kummerSelmerMap τ) ⇑(φ.selmerShaMap τ)`: the kernel of $\mathrm{Sel}_\varphi \to Ш(E_1)[\varphi]$ is the image of the Kummer map $E_2(K)/\varphi(E_1(K)) \to \mathrm{Sel}_\varphi$.

This is the exactness at the middle term of the standard $\varphi$-descent sequence $0 \to E_2(K)/\varphi(E_1(K)) \to \mathrm{Sel}_\varphi \to Ш(E_1)[\varphi] \to 0$. Over a number field, with the $L_i$ its completions, the groups are the classical ones; exactness at the Selmer group does not depend on which local conditions cut it out, so it holds for every family.

## References and tests
- Silverman, AEC X.4.2(a) — the $\varphi$-descent exact sequence, of which this theorem is the exactness at the Selmer group.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `Function.Exact f g` says that, for every $y$, $g(y) = 0$ exactly when $y$ is in the image of $f$: exactness at the middle term only. Injectivity of the Kummer map and surjectivity onto $Ш(E_1)[\varphi]$ are separate statements.
- The Selmer and Shafarevich–Tate groups are taken relative to the family of the $L_i$ with the embeddings $\tau_i$; the classical groups are one case.
- The cohomology is the continuous cohomology of `AbsoluteGaloisGroup K`, the automorphisms of a separable closure $K^{\mathrm{sep}}$ of $K$, with coefficients the points over $K^{\mathrm{sep}}$. Separability of $\varphi$ is what makes $\varphi$ onto on those points, as the Kummer map needs; in characteristic $0$ every isogeny is separable.
- `W₁.toAffine` is the same curve in affine coordinates, the form `Isogeny` takes; `⇑` turns a homomorphism into its underlying function.
- The hypotheses in square brackets are carried as typeclasses, found by Lean itself. $K$ is any field, and nothing is claimed about finiteness.

## What it says
`mulByIntIsogeny W hn` is the multiplication-by-$n$ map $[n] : E \to E$, $P \mapsto nP$, of an elliptic curve, as a nonzero isogeny, for an integer $n$ whose division polynomial is not zero as a function on the curve.

- `[Field F]`: $F$ is a field; `Field` is the class of fields.
- `(W : WeierstrassCurve.Affine F)`: a Weierstrass equation `W` over $F$.
- `[WeierstrassCurve.IsElliptic W]`: its discriminant is a unit, so `W` defines an elliptic curve $E$.
- `(hn : psiFunctionField W n ≠ 0)`: for the integer $n$ (an implicit argument), the $n$-th division polynomial $\psi_n$, read in the function field $F(W)$, that is, at the generic point of the curve, is not zero.
- The result is an `Isogeny W W`: a nonzero isogeny from $E$ to itself.

Its value has two parts: the pullback `mulByIntPullback W hn`, which sends the coordinates $x$, $y$ to $\phi_n/\psi_n^2$ and $\omega_n/\psi_n^3$, the coordinates of $[n](x, y)$ by the division-polynomial formulas; and `mapsInfinity_mulByIntPullback W hn`, the proof that the origin goes to the origin. These are the standard formulas for $[n]$, so this is the standard multiplication map, recorded through its action on functions.

## References and tests
- [Blueprint `ec.endomorphism_ring`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.endomorphism_ring) — the copy of the integers in the endomorphism ring, given by $P \mapsto nP$, whose nonzero part this definition provides.
- `TauCeti.Isogeny.mulByIntIsogeny_pullback` — passes: the pullback of this isogeny is the division-polynomial pullback.

The test records that the isogeny is the division-polynomial map and nothing else, so its properties are those of the classical formulas.

## Lean subtleties
- Since $\psi_0 = 0$, the hypothesis excludes $n = 0$: the zero map is no `Isogeny`, which holds only nonzero isogenies. For $n \neq 0$, $\psi_n$ is a nonzero function, since $[n]$ is not constant, so every nonzero $n$, negative ones included, qualifies; the construction divides by $\psi_n$, which is why the hypothesis is stated in this form.
- The hypothesis concerns $\psi_n$ as a function, not its value at each point: at the points of the kernel of $[n]$ it vanishes, and those points go to the point at infinity.
- For $n = 1$, $\psi_1 = 1$, $\phi_1 = x$ and $\omega_1 = y$, so the pullback is the identity.
- `[WeierstrassCurve.IsElliptic W]` is a hypothesis carried as a typeclass, found by Lean itself; $F$ is any field, of any characteristic. `noncomputable` does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
`P.ordAddMonoidHom` is the valuation of a place $P$, the order of vanishing $\mathrm{ord}_P$, as a group homomorphism from the multiplicative group $F^\times$ of nonzero elements to $\mathbb{Z}$.

- `[Field k] [Field F] [Algebra k F]`: $k$ and $F$ are fields and $F$ is an extension of $k$ (the `Algebra` structure).
- `(P : Place k F)`: a place `P` of $F/k$: a normalized discrete valuation of $F$ that is trivial on the constants $k$.
- The result, `Additive Fˣ →+ ℤ`: a homomorphism of additive groups from `Additive Fˣ`, the group $F^\times$ with its multiplication written as addition, to $\mathbb{Z}$.

Its value sends a nonzero $z$ to $\mathrm{ord}_P(z)$, the order function of the place, normalized so that a prime element has order $1$. It is a homomorphism because $\mathrm{ord}_P(zw) = \mathrm{ord}_P(z) + \mathrm{ord}_P(w)$ for nonzero $z$, $w$. This is the standard discrete valuation $v_P$ restricted to $F^\times$, where it is a homomorphism by the product axiom of a valuation; the value $v_P(0) = \infty$ lies outside, as $0$ is no unit.

## References and tests
- Stichtenoth, Definition 1.1.12 — the discrete valuation of a function field, whose product rule makes its restriction to $F^\times$ a homomorphism to $\mathbb{Z}$.
- `TauCeti.Place.ordAddMonoidHom_apply` — passes: on a nonzero $z$, the homomorphism gives $\mathrm{ord}_P(z)$.
- `TauCeti.Place.orderSystem_ord` — passes: for a function field, the order system that divisors are built from takes the value $\mathrm{ord}_P(z)$ at $P$ on each nonzero $z$.

The tests pin the map down to the order function on every nonzero element, and show it is the one that divisors use.

## Lean subtleties
- `Fˣ` is the group of units of $F$, its nonzero elements; `Additive` writes its product as a sum, so the homomorphism law reads $\mathrm{ord}_P(z + w) = \mathrm{ord}_P(z) + \mathrm{ord}_P(w)$ with $z + w$ meaning the product in $F$.
- `Place.ord` takes the junk value $\mathrm{ord}_P(0) = 0$ where the classical valuation is $\infty$, and it is not additive there; restricting to units leaves that value out.
- The normalization is the standard one: a prime element of the place has order $1$, and the nonzero constants have order $0$.
- No hypothesis asks that $F$ be a function field over $k$; the tests that need it assume it. `noncomputable` does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
`ReductionSymbol` is the type of Kodaira symbols, the labels of the reduction types of an elliptic curve at a prime, as Tate's algorithm outputs them. It takes no arguments; its elements are given by its constructors:

- `I n`, for a natural number $n$: the symbol $I_n$. Here $I_0$ is good reduction and $I_n$ with $n \ge 1$ is multiplicative reduction.
- `II`, `III`, `IV`: the additive symbols $\mathrm{II}$, $\mathrm{III}$, $\mathrm{IV}$.
- `IStar n`, for a natural number $n$: the additive symbol $I_n^*$, with $I_0^*$ at $n = 0$.
- `IVStar`, `IIIStar`, `IIStar`: the additive symbols $\mathrm{IV}^*$, $\mathrm{III}^*$, $\mathrm{II}^*$.

This is the standard list of Kodaira–Néron types: two infinite families, $I_n$ and $I_n^*$ for $n \ge 0$, and six exceptional types. Each symbol has exactly one constructor, so the elements of the type correspond one to one to the symbols.

## References and tests
- [Blueprint `ec.q.kodaira_symbol`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.q.kodaira_symbol) — the Kodaira symbol of an elliptic curve at a prime, whose vocabulary of labels this type lists.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- In an inductive type, values built from different constructors, or from one constructor with different arguments, are different. So `I 0` ($I_0$, good reduction) and `IStar 0` ($I_0^*$, additive) are distinct, and so are $I_m$ and $I_n$ for $m \ne n$.
- The index $n$ is a natural number, starting at $0$: no negative index is admitted, and the zero cases are the first members of the families rather than constructors of their own.
- The type holds the labels only: it does not say which label a given curve has, nor whether multiplicative reduction is split or nonsplit, which the symbol $I_n$ does not record.
- `deriving DecidableEq, Repr` makes equality of symbols decidable and lets them be printed; it adds no mathematics.
- The names spell the stars out: `IStar n` is $I_n^*$, `IVStar` is $\mathrm{IV}^*$, `IIIStar` is $\mathrm{III}^*$ and `IIStar` is $\mathrm{II}^*$.

## What it says
`TateModule p A` is the $p$-adic Tate module $T_p(A)$ of an abelian group $A$: the compatible families of $p^n$-torsion elements, that is, the inverse limit of the groups $A[p^n]$ under multiplication by $p$.

- `(p : ℕ)`: a natural number `p`, a prime in the intended use.
- `[AddCommGroup A]`: the type `A` is an abelian group, written additively.
- The result is a type: the elements of the Tate module.

Its value is `tateModuleSubgroup p A`: the subgroup of the product $\prod_{n \ge 0} A[p^n]$, where $A[p^n] = \{a \in A : p^n a = 0\}$, made of the families $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$ with $p\,x_{n+1} = x_n$ for every $n$. This is the standard construction $T_p(A) = \varprojlim_n A[p^n]$, with multiplication by $p$ as the transition maps; for an elliptic curve $E$, applied to its points over an algebraic closure, it is the Tate module $T_p(E)$.

## References and tests
- [Blueprint `ec.padic_tate_module`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.padic_tate_module) — the $p$-adic Tate module of an elliptic curve, the inverse limit of the groups $E[p^n]$ under multiplication by $p$.
- `TauCeti.tateModuleTransition_apply` — passes: the transition map from $A[p^{n+1}]$ to $A[p^n]$ is multiplication by $p$.
- `TauCeti.mem_tateModuleSubgroup_iff` — passes: a family lies in the Tate module exactly when each component is $p$ times the next.

Together the tests give the inverse-limit condition in its classical form, with the classical transition maps.

## Lean subtleties
- `TateModule p A` is a type, the elements of the subgroup; its addition comes from the subgroup. No topology and no $\mathbb{Z}_p$-module structure is part of this definition.
- The level $n = 0$ is $A[1] = \{0\}$, so $x_0 = 0$ and that level imposes no condition.
- Nothing asks that `p` be prime. For $p = 1$ every level is $\{0\}$, and for $p = 0$ the condition forces $x_n = 0 \cdot x_{n+1} = 0$; in both cases the Tate module is zero.
- `A` is any abelian group. For an elliptic curve over $K$, the classical Tate module is the case of the points over an algebraic closure of $K$; applied to the $K$-rational points alone, the result can be smaller.
- `Type u_1`: the Tate module lies in the universe of $A$, which does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
Let $W$ be a Weierstrass curve over a nonarchimedean local field $K$ that acquires good reduction over a finite extension $L$ of $K$. If $\sigma$ is in the inertia group of $K$ and fixes $L$, and $p \nmid n$ for the residue characteristic $p$, then $\sigma$ fixes every point $P$ over $\bar K$ such that $\sigma(nP) = nP$.

- `[Field K] [ValuativeRel K] [TopologicalSpace K] [IsNonarchimedeanLocalField K]`: $K$ is a nonarchimedean local field, with its valuation and topology.
- `[Field L] [ValuativeRel L] [TopologicalSpace L] [IsNonarchimedeanLocalField L]`: so is $L$.
- `[Algebra K L] [ValuativeExtension K L] [FiniteDimensional K L]`: $L$ is a finite extension of $K$ whose valuation extends that of $K$.
- `(ι : L →ₐ[K] AlgebraicClosure K)`: an embedding `ι` of $L$ over $K$ into an algebraic closure $\bar K$.
- `(C : VariableChange L)`: a change of variables `C` over $L$.
- `[IsIntegral (↥(ValuativeRel.valuation L).integer) (C • W.baseChange L)]`: the equation $C \cdot W$ over $L$ has coefficients in the valuation ring $\mathcal{O}_L$.
- `[(integralModel (↥(ValuativeRel.valuation L).integer) (C • W.baseChange L)).IsElliptic]`: as an equation over $\mathcal{O}_L$, its discriminant is a unit there: $W$ has good reduction over $L$.
- `[DecidableEq (AlgebraicClosure K)]`: equality in $\bar K$ can be decided, which the group law uses; technical.
- `(hn : ↑n ≠ 0)`: the natural number $n$ is nonzero in the residue field of $K$, that is, $p \nmid n$.
- `(hσ : σ ∈ TauCeti.inertiaSubgroup K)`: $\sigma \in \mathrm{Gal}(\bar K/K)$ lies in the inertia subgroup $I_K$.
- `(hσL : σ ∈ ι.fieldRange.fixingSubgroup)`: $\sigma$ fixes $\iota(L)$ pointwise, so it lies in the inertia group of $L$.
- `(hP : (map ↑σ) (n • P) = n • P)`: for a point $P \in W(\bar K)$, $\sigma$ fixes $nP$.
- The conclusion, `(map ↑σ) P = P`: $\sigma$ fixes $P$.

Taking $nP = O$, $\sigma$ fixes $E[n]$: prime-to-$p$ torsion is unramified over a field of good reduction, the classical result applied over $L$. The general case is what its proof gives: $\sigma P - P$ is $n$-torsion and reduces to $O$, and reduction is injective on such torsion.

## References and tests
- Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, VII.4.1(a) — torsion of order prime to the residue characteristic is unramified at good reduction; this theorem is that result over $L$, in the form its proof gives.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- In `hn`, the printed `↑n` is $n$ cast into the residue field of $K$; the condition also excludes $n = 0$.
- `map ↑σ` applies $\sigma$ to the coordinates of a point; `n • P` is $nP$. The type of points includes the point at infinity $O$.
- Good reduction over $L$ is expressed by an integral model with unit discriminant after the change of variables `C`, so $W$ need only have potentially good reduction over $K$.
- The hypotheses in square brackets are carried as typeclasses, found by Lean itself.

## What it says
`W.PointModTorsion` is the group of points of a Weierstrass curve over $F$ modulo its torsion: $E(F)/E(F)_{\mathrm{tors}}$, the Mordell–Weil group with its points of finite order divided out.

- `[Field F]`: $F$ is a field; `Field` is the class of fields.
- `(W : Affine F)`: a Weierstrass equation `W` over $F$, in affine coordinates.
- `[DecidableEq F]`: equality in $F$ can be decided, which the group law on points uses to tell its cases apart; a technical hypothesis.
- The result is a type: the quotient group.

Its value is `W.Point ⧸ Submodule.torsion ℤ W.Point`: the group `W.Point` of points of `W` with coordinates in $F$, together with the point at infinity, viewed as a module over $\mathbb{Z}$, divided by its torsion submodule, the points $P$ with $mP = O$ for some nonzero integer $m$. Two points have the same class exactly when they differ by a point of finite order.

This is the standard quotient $E(F)/E(F)_{\mathrm{tors}}$. Over a number field, where the Mordell–Weil theorem gives $E(F) \cong \mathbb{Z}^r \oplus E(F)_{\mathrm{tors}}$, it is free of rank $r$, the rank of $E$, and a basis of it is the non-torsion part of a set of Mordell–Weil generators.

## References and tests
- [Blueprint `ec.mw_generators`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.mw_generators) — the generators of the Mordell–Weil group, whose non-torsion part is a basis of this quotient.
- `WeierstrassCurve.Affine.fg_point_of_numberField` — passes: for an elliptic curve over a number field, the group of points is finitely generated, the Mordell–Weil theorem.

With the test, this quotient is a finitely generated abelian group without torsion over a number field, hence free of finite rank, as the classical theory has it.

## Lean subtleties
- `Submodule.torsion ℤ` treats the abelian group of points as a module over $\mathbb{Z}$; its torsion is the set of elements killed by a nonzero integer, the points of finite order.
- No hypothesis asks that `W` be an elliptic curve: for a singular equation, `W.Point` is the group of its nonsingular points.
- No finiteness is assumed: over a field such as an algebraically closed one the quotient need not be finitely generated; the finite rank is the number-field case.
- `abbrev` makes the definition unfold automatically, so the quotient carries the group structure of a quotient module; `⧸` is Lean's notation for a quotient.

## What it says
`W.canonicalHeightQuadratic` is the canonical (Néron–Tate) height $\hat h$ on the points of an elliptic curve, packaged as a quadratic form over $\mathbb{Z}$ with real values.

- `[Field F]`: $F$ is a field; `Field` is the class of fields.
- `(W : Affine F)`: a Weierstrass equation `W` over $F$, in affine coordinates.
- `[Height.AdmissibleAbsValues F]`: $F$ carries an admissible family of absolute values, which defines the naive height of its elements, such as the usual absolute values of $\mathbb{Q}$.
- `[DecidableEq F]`: equality in $F$ can be decided, which the group law on points uses; a technical hypothesis.
- `[WeierstrassCurve.IsElliptic (toAffine W)]`: the discriminant of `W` is a unit, so `W` is an elliptic curve $E$.
- The result, `QuadraticMap ℤ W.Point ℝ`: a quadratic map $q$ from the group $E(F)$ of points, a module over $\mathbb{Z}$, to $\mathbb{R}$: $q(mP) = m^2 q(P)$ for every integer $m$, and $q(P + Q) - q(P) - q(Q)$ is additive in each variable.

Its value is built by `TauCeti.QuadraticMap.ofParallelogram` from the parallelogram law $\hat h(P+Q) + \hat h(P-Q) = 2\hat h(P) + 2\hat h(Q)$, and takes the value $\hat h(P) = \lim_n h_x(2^n P)/4^n$ at $P$, where $h_x$ is the naive height of the $x$-coordinate. That the canonical height is a quadratic form on $E(F)$ is the standard theorem; this is its statement as a single object.

## References and tests
- [the LeanBridge/LMFDB knowl](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.q.canonical_height) — the canonical height of a point of an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$.
- `WeierstrassCurve.Affine.canonicalHeightQuadratic_apply` — passes: at each point the quadratic map takes the value $\hat h(P)$.
- `WeierstrassCurve.Affine.neronTatePairing_self` — passes: the associated Néron–Tate pairing has $\hat h(P)$ on its diagonal, $\langle P, P\rangle = \hat h(P)$.

The first test shows that the packaging changes no value; the second fixes the factor of two between this quadratic map and its pairing.

## Lean subtleties
- Normalisation: $\hat h(P) = \lim_n h_x(2^n P)/4^n$, without the factor $\tfrac12$ that some texts put in front.
- The polar form of a quadratic map is $q(P+Q) - q(P) - q(Q)$, twice the Néron–Tate pairing; it is half of it that has $\hat h$ on its diagonal.
- The naive height, and with it $\hat h$, is taken relative to the family of absolute values the instance supplies; over a number field, its normalisation follows that family.
- The point group is a $\mathbb{Z}$-module, not a vector space. Nothing asserts positivity: $\hat h$ is zero on points of finite order, as any quadratic map is.
- `noncomputable` does not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
The Mordell–Weil theorem for elliptic curves: if $E$ is an elliptic curve over a number field $F$, the group $E(F)$ of its $F$-rational points is finitely generated.

- `[Field F] [NumberField F]`: $F$ is a number field, a field of characteristic $0$ that is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb{Q}$.
- `[DecidableEq F]`: equality of elements of $F$ can be decided, which the formulas of the group law use to branch; it adds no mathematical hypothesis.
- `[WeierstrassCurve.IsElliptic (toAffine W)]`: the Weierstrass equation $W$ over $F$, given implicitly, with coefficients $a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4, a_6$, has discriminant a unit of $F$, that is $\Delta \neq 0$, so that it defines an elliptic curve $E$.
- The conclusion: `Module.Finite ℤ W.Point`, the group `W.Point` of points of $E$ over $F$, the point at infinity included as its zero, is finitely generated as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module, that is, as an abelian group: there are points $P_1, \dots, P_n$ such that every point is $m_1 P_1 + \dots + m_n P_n$ for some integers $m_i$.

This is the Mordell–Weil theorem as it is usually stated for an elliptic curve over a number field, with no extra hypothesis, and for every Weierstrass model, not only a short or a minimal one. With the structure of finitely generated abelian groups it gives $E(F) \cong T \oplus \mathbb{Z}^r$ with $T$ finite, so that the rank $r$ of $E(F)$ is finite.

## References and tests
- LeanBridge’s `ec.mordell_weil_theorem` — the blueprint's statement of the Mordell–Weil theorem ([source](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.mordell_weil_theorem)), which this instance states for $\mathbb{Z}$-modules.
- `WeierstrassCurve.Affine.fg_point_of_numberField` — passes: under the same hypotheses, the point group is finitely generated as an additive group; the instance is this theorem in the language of $\mathbb{Z}$-modules.
- `TauCeti.WorkedExamples.finrank_point_curve37a1_pos` — passes: for the curve 37.a1 over $\mathbb{Q}$, the rank of its point group as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module is positive.
- `TauCeti.WorkedExamples.finrank_point_curveX3SubXAddOne` — passes: for the curve $y^2 = x^3 - x + 1$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, that rank is exactly $1$.

The first test is the theorem itself, in group language, for every elliptic curve over every number field; the two worked curves show that the rank this instance makes finite is computed as expected, and is not always $0$.

## Lean subtleties
- `Module.Finite ℤ W.Point` means finitely generated over $\mathbb{Z}$, not finite: `W.Point` is often an infinite set, and $\mathbb{Z}$ acts on it by repeated addition in the group law. It does not say that the curve is defined over $\mathbb{Z}$.
- `W : Affine F` is the Weierstrass equation read in affine coordinates, but `W.Point` is the whole group $E(F)$: besides the affine solutions it has the point at infinity, its zero.
- The hypotheses in square brackets are typeclasses, which Lean finds by itself. `WeierstrassCurve.IsElliptic` asks that the discriminant be a unit, which in a field means nonzero.
- `[DecidableEq F]` is technical: classically every field has decidable equality, so it restricts nothing.
- Since it is an instance, Lean uses it automatically. Lean's rank `Module.finrank ℤ W.Point` is defined to be $0$ for a module of infinite rank; this instance is what makes it the rank $r$ of $E(F)$.

## What it says
The Néron–Tate pairing $\langle P, Q \rangle$ of an elliptic curve $E$ over a field $F$ that has a theory of heights, passed to the quotient $E(F)/E(F)_{\mathrm{tors}}$ of its group of points by the torsion subgroup.

- `[Field F]`: $F$ is a field.
- `(W : Affine F)`: a Weierstrass equation $W$ over $F$, read in affine coordinates.
- `[Height.AdmissibleAbsValues F]`: $F$ carries an admissible family of absolute values, the data from which heights on $F$ are built, as from the places of a number field.
- `[DecidableEq F]`: equality in $F$ can be decided; a technical hypothesis.
- `[WeierstrassCurve.IsElliptic (toAffine W)]`: the discriminant of $W$ is a unit, that is nonzero, so $W$ defines an elliptic curve $E$.
- The value: a $\mathbb{Z}$-bilinear form with real values on `W.PointModTorsion`, the group $E(F)$ modulo its torsion. It is `LinearMap.IsRefl.liftQ₂` applied to `WeierstrassCurve.Affine.neronTatePairing`, the Néron–Tate pairing on $E(F)$: on classes $[P], [Q]$ it takes the value $\langle P, Q \rangle$. This is well defined because the pairing is reflexive ($\langle P, Q \rangle = 0$ implies $\langle Q, P \rangle = 0$) and every torsion point $T$ has $\langle T, Q \rangle = 0$ for all $Q$, so changing a representative by a torsion point leaves the value unchanged.

The Néron–Tate pairing vanishes on torsion and is usually regarded on $E(F)$ modulo torsion, where over a number field it is positive definite and its Gram determinant on a basis is the regulator. This declaration is that descended form, with the normalisation of `WeierstrassCurve.Affine.neronTatePairing`; it gives the pairing, not the regulator.

## References and tests
- LeanBridge/LMFDB knowl — on the regulator of an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ ([ec.q.regulator](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.q.regulator)), which is computed from this pairing on $E(\mathbb{Q})$ modulo torsion.
- `WeierstrassCurve.Affine.neronTatePairingModTorsion_mk` — passes: on the classes of points $P$ and $Q$, the pairing is $\langle P, Q \rangle$, the Néron–Tate pairing of the representatives.
- `WeierstrassCurve.Affine.neronTatePairingModTorsion_self_eq_zero_iff` — passes: when the canonical height has the Northcott property (finitely many points of bounded height), $\langle x, x \rangle = 0$ only for the zero class $x$.

The first test says that the descended form is the Néron–Tate pairing and nothing else; the second, that under the Northcott property dividing by torsion removes exactly the points on which the form vanishes, as in the classical theory.

## Lean subtleties
- `LinearMap.BilinMap ℤ W.PointModTorsion ℝ` is the type of $\mathbb{Z}$-bilinear maps to $\mathbb{R}$: biadditive maps, $\mathbb{Z}$ acting on points by repeated addition. It is not yet a form on the real vector space $E(F) \otimes \mathbb{R}$.
- `W.PointModTorsion` is the quotient by `Submodule.torsion ℤ W.Point`, the points killed by some nonzero integer; `W.Point` includes the point at infinity, the zero of the group.
- `liftQ₂` evaluates on a pair of classes through representatives; the inclusion of the torsion in the kernel, which the definition receives as a proof, makes the value independent of them, so no choice is made.
- `[Height.AdmissibleAbsValues F]` is a typeclass: Lean finds the family of absolute values by itself, and the heights, hence the pairing, depend on it. It lets the definition apply beyond number fields.
- Nothing here asserts positive definiteness: the definition holds for every such $F$, and the second test needs the Northcott property for its conclusion.
- `noncomputable` says only that Lean cannot evaluate it, as is usual for real-valued definitions.

## What it says
For a Weierstrass equation $W$ with integral coefficients over a valued field $F$, the subgroup $E_0(F)$ of the points of $W$ over $F$ whose reduction is a nonsingular point of the reduced curve.

- `[Field F]`: $F$ is a field.
- `[LinearOrderedCommGroupWithZero Γ₀]`: $\Gamma_0$ is a linearly ordered commutative group with a zero adjoined, written multiplicatively; it receives the values of the valuation.
- `(v : Valuation F Γ₀)`: a valuation $v$ on $F$ with values in $\Gamma_0$, written multiplicatively: $v(xy) = v(x)v(y)$ and $v(x + y) \le \max(v(x), v(y))$. Its valuation ring is $\mathcal{O}_v = \{x : v(x) \le 1\}$, with residue field $k$.
- `(W : Affine F)`: a Weierstrass equation $y^2 + a_1xy + a_3y = x^3 + a_2x^2 + a_4x + a_6$ over $F$, read in affine coordinates.
- `[IsIntegral (↥v.valuationSubring) W]`: its coefficients $a_i$ lie in $\mathcal{O}_v$.
- `[DecidableEq F]`: equality in $F$ can be decided; a technical hypothesis.
- The value: the additive subgroup of `W.Point`, the group of points of $W$ over $F$, made of the points $P$ whose reduction $\tilde P$, a point of the projective plane over $k$, is a nonsingular point of the curve $\tilde W$ over $k$ whose coefficients are those of $W$ reduced modulo the maximal ideal. The proofs in the value show that the point at infinity lies in it and that it is closed under addition and negation.

This is the subgroup $E_0$ of points with nonsingular reduction of the theory of reduction of elliptic curves, here relative to the given integral equation $W$ and for any valuation, discrete or not.

## References and tests
- The Tamagawa-number knowl — in the LeanBridge blueprint ([`ec.tamagawa_number`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.tamagawa_number)), it defines the Tamagawa number at a place with the subgroup of points with smooth reduction; for a minimal equation over the completed local field, the Tamagawa number is the index of this subgroup.
- `WeierstrassCurve.Affine.mem_nonsingularReduction_of_one_lt` — passes: a point $P$ whose $x$-coordinate has a pole, $v(x(P)) > 1$, lies in the subgroup.

The test shows that the reduction is taken in projective coordinates: such a point reduces to the point at infinity, which is nonsingular, and is not discarded as it would be by a test on integral affine coordinates.

## Lean subtleties
- Valuations are multiplicative in Lean: $v(x) \le 1$ means that $x$ is integral, and $v(x) > 1$ that $x$ has a pole, which additively is a negative valuation.
- The subgroup depends on the equation $W$, not only on the curve: for an integral equation that is not minimal it can be another subgroup. The usual $E_0$ is taken for a minimal equation.
- No ellipticity is assumed: `W.Point` is the group of nonsingular points of $W$ over $F$, the point at infinity included as its zero, whether or not the discriminant vanishes.
- `[IsIntegral (↥v.valuationSubring) W]` is a hypothesis carried as a typeclass, which Lean finds by itself; `↥v.valuationSubring` is the valuation ring $\mathcal{O}_v$ seen as a ring of its own.
- The reduction is a point class of the projective plane: its coordinates are defined up to a common unit factor, so no representative is chosen.
- `noncomputable` says only that Lean does not evaluate it.

## What it says
The Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture for an elliptic curve $E$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, as a proposition: the declaration states it and proves nothing. It is asserted for curves whose Shafarevich–Tate group is finite.

- `(E : WeierstrassCurve ℚ)`: a Weierstrass equation $E$ with rational coefficients.
- `[E.IsElliptic]`: its discriminant is a unit of $\mathbb{Q}$, that is nonzero, so $E$ is an elliptic curve.
- The value: the proposition that, if the Shafarevich–Tate group `E.sha` is finite, then for every function $f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every set $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ such that $f$ is an analytic continuation to $U$ of the $L$-series $L(E, s) = \sum_n a_n n^{-s}$ of $E$ (`LSeries.IsAnalyticContinuation`: $U$ is open and connected, $f$ is analytic on $U$, and $U$ meets the half-plane where the series converges) and $1 \in U$:
  - the order of vanishing of $f$ at $s = 1$, `analyticOrderAt f 1`, equals the rank $r$ of $E(\mathbb{Q})$, `Module.finrank ℤ E.toAffine.Point`;
  - the leading Taylor coefficient $f^{(r)}(1)/r!$ equals `E.bsdQuotient`, the Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer quotient of $E$, defined when Sha is finite: the value the conjecture predicts for it.

These are the two predictions of the conjecture, the rank and the leading coefficient. Both are stated under the hypothesis that Sha is finite, which the leading coefficient needs to make sense; the finiteness of Sha is a hypothesis here, not a claim, and the existence of a continuation is not part of the statement.

## References and tests
- Wiles, Clay description — the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture as the Clay Mathematics Institute's problem description states it: the rank and the leading coefficient.

No test is recorded for it: it is a conjecture, stated and not proved.

## Lean subtleties
- `∀ [Finite E.sha]` writes the hypothesis that Sha is finite in the square brackets of a typeclass. `E.sha` is the Shafarevich–Tate group, a subgroup of the first Galois cohomology group of the points of $E$ over a separable closure of $\mathbb{Q}$.
- The statement quantifies over every analytic continuation $f$ and does not assert that one exists. By modularity $L(E,s)$ extends to an entire function, and every such $f$ agrees with it on $U$, so the statement is about $L(E,s)$ near $s = 1$.
- `analyticOrderAt f 1` takes values in $\mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, with $\infty$ when $f$ vanishes near $1$; the rank, a natural number, is cast there.
- `Module.finrank ℤ E.toAffine.Point` is Lean's rank of $E(\mathbb{Q})$, the point at infinity included; it would be $0$ for a group of infinite rank, but $E(\mathbb{Q})$ is finitely generated by the Mordell–Weil theorem.
- The coefficients of `E.LFunction` are integers, cast to $\mathbb{C}$ by `(↑)`; the docstring calls this $L$-series `WeierstrassCurve.LSeries E`.
- `iteratedDeriv` is the complex $r$-th derivative, and the division by $r!$ is in $\mathbb{C}$, where the real number `E.bsdQuotient` is read.
- When $r = 0$ the claims are $f(1) \neq 0$ and $f(1) =$ `E.bsdQuotient`.

## What it says
The geometric endomorphism ring of a Weierstrass curve $W$ over a field $F$: the endomorphisms of $W$ after base change to a separable closure $F^{\mathrm{sep}}$ of $F$. The declaration gives its underlying type.

- `[Field F]`: $F$ is a field.
- `(W : WeierstrassCurve F)`: a Weierstrass equation $W$ over $F$, with coefficients $a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4, a_6$.
- The value: `Hom` from the base change of $W$ to $F^{\mathrm{sep}}$, read in affine coordinates, to itself. This is the type `TauCeti.Isogeny.Hom` of maps of the curve to itself over $F^{\mathrm{sep}}$, each recorded by its action on functions: a linear multiplicative map out of the coordinate ring, pointed wherever it is unital.

For an elliptic curve this is the usual geometric endomorphism ring, the endomorphisms over $F^{\mathrm{sep}}$; in characteristic $0$ the separable closure is an algebraic closure, so it is $\operatorname{End}_{\bar F}(E)$. As the docstring says, it contains the endomorphisms defined over $F$, through base change, and may be strictly larger.

## References and tests
- The Q-endomorphism knowl — in the LeanBridge blueprint ([`ec.q.endomorphism_ring`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.q.endomorphism_ring)), it separates the endomorphisms defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ from those that appear only over a field extension; this declaration is the second, geometric ring.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- It is an `abbrev`: a name for the type `Hom` above, which Lean unfolds, so what Lean knows of `Hom`, its ring structure included, applies to it.
- `SeparableClosure F` is one separable closure of $F$, built inside Lean's algebraic closure `AlgebraicClosure F`; another choice would give an isomorphic ring.
- No ellipticity is assumed: the type exists for every Weierstrass equation, singular ones included.
- `Type u_1`: the result is a type in the same universe as $F$, which has no bearing on the mathematics.
- The endomorphisms over $F$ map into it by base change, `TauCeti.Isogeny.Hom.mapRingHom` in the docstring. For a curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ with complex multiplication, the endomorphisms over $\mathbb{Q}$ are only the multiplications by integers, while this ring is an order in an imaginary quadratic field.

## What it says
A Weierstrass equation $W$ over the fraction field $K$ of a discrete valuation ring $R$ has good supersingular reduction at $p$ when it is minimal, has good reduction, and its reduction over the residue field $k$ of $R$ is a supersingular curve at $p$.

- `[CommRing R] [IsDomain R] [IsDiscreteValuationRing R]`: $R$ is a discrete valuation ring, with residue field $k$.
- `[Field K] [Algebra R K] [IsFractionRing R K]`: $K$ is the fraction field of $R$.
- `(p : ℕ)`: a natural number $p$, meant, as the docstring says, to be the characteristic of $k$.
- `(W : WeierstrassCurve K)`: a Weierstrass equation $W$ over $K$.
- `extends WeierstrassCurve.HasGoodReduction R W`: the class contains `HasGoodReduction R W`: $W$ is a minimal equation with respect to $R$, and its discriminant is a unit of $R$.
- The field `isSupersingular_reduction`: `(W.reduction R).IsSupersingular p`, the reduced equation $\tilde W$ over $k$ is supersingular at $p$: it has no nonzero point $P$ with $pP = 0$ over an algebraic closure of $k$.

This is good supersingular reduction as in the local theory of elliptic curves: good reduction, with a reduced curve whose $p$-torsion over an algebraic closure of $k$ is trivial, as opposed to ordinary reduction.

## References and tests
- LMFDB knowl — on good supersingular reduction, [`ec.good_supersingular_reduction`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.good_supersingular_reduction) in the LeanBridge blueprint: its two conditions, good reduction and a supersingular reduced curve, are the two parts of this class.
- `WeierstrassCurve.hasGoodSupersingularReduction_iff_dvd_frobeniusTrace` — passes: when $k$ is finite of characteristic $p$ and $W$ has good reduction, $W$ has good supersingular reduction exactly when $p$ divides the trace of Frobenius of the reduced curve.

The test is the classical criterion for a curve over a finite field of characteristic $p$ to be supersingular, so the class means here what it means in the literature.

## Lean subtleties
- It is a `class` whose values are propositions: `HasGoodSupersingularReduction R p W` holds when both its parts hold, and Lean can find it by itself as an instance.
- Minimality is part of it, through `HasGoodReduction`, which extends `IsMinimal`: it is a property of the equation $W$, and fails for an equation that is not minimal, even of a curve with good supersingular reduction.
- Valuations are multiplicative in Lean: the docstring of `HasGoodReduction`, a discriminant of valuation $1$, means a unit of $R$, of additive valuation $0$.
- The class does not tie $p$ to the characteristic of $k$; it is meant for $p$ equal to it, and the test takes $p$ so, through `ExpChar`, for a finite residue field.
- `W.reduction R` is the equation with its coefficients reduced to `IsLocalRing.ResidueField R`, the residue field $k$; it is defined for minimal equations, which the class provides.

## What it says
A Weierstrass equation $W$ over a field $K$ has potential good reduction at the place given by $R$ when, after some finite extension $L$ of $K$ and at a discrete valuation ring of $L$ lying over $R$, a minimal equation of $W$ has good reduction.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring; it is meant to be a discrete valuation ring, the local ring of the place at which reduction is taken.
- `[Field K] [Algebra R K]`: $K$ is a field with a ring map $R \to K$, as when $K$ is the fraction field of $R$.
- `(W : WeierstrassCurve K)`: a Weierstrass equation $W$ over $K$.
- The value: there exist a field $L$ finite-dimensional over $K$, and a discrete valuation ring $S$ with fraction field $L$ with a ring map $R \to S$ that is local (`IsLocalHom`: an element of $R$ whose image is a unit of $S$ is a unit of $R$, so that $S$ dominates $R$), such that
  - the maps $R \to S \to L$ and $R \to K \to L$ agree, so that $S$ lies over $R$ inside $L$;
  - the minimal equation over $S$ of $W$ base-changed to $L$ has good reduction: its discriminant is a unit of $S$.

This is the usual local notion: the curve acquires good reduction over a finite extension, at a place above the given one. Over a discrete valuation ring it agrees with the classical criterion of an integral $j$-invariant, as the first test shows.

## References and tests
- LeanBridge/LMFDB knowl — on potential good reduction, [`ec.potential_good_reduction`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.potential_good_reduction); it is global, asking for good reduction everywhere over a finite extension of a number field, and this declaration is its local ingredient at one place.
- `WeierstrassCurve.hasPotentialGoodReduction_iff_isInteger_j` — passes: for $R$ a discrete valuation ring with fraction field $K$ and $W$ elliptic, $W$ has potential good reduction exactly when its $j$-invariant lies in $R$.
- `WeierstrassCurve.hasPotentialGoodReduction_smul` — passes: a change of variables over $K$ does not change it, so it depends on the curve, not on the equation.

The first test is the classical characterisation; the second shows that the definition does not depend on the equation chosen.

## Lean subtleties
- The existential runs over types $L$ and $S$ with their structures: the anonymous witnesses `(_ : Field L)`, `(_ : IsDiscreteValuationRing S)` and the others say that $L$ is a field, $S$ a discrete valuation ring, and so on.
- The minimal equation is taken after base change to $L$: an equation minimal over $K$ need not stay minimal over $L$.
- $R$ is any commutative ring, and $K$ need not be its fraction field: the definition is meant for $R$ a discrete valuation ring with fraction field $K$, which the first test assumes.
- Valuations are multiplicative in Lean: `HasGoodReduction`'s discriminant of valuation $1$ is a unit of $S$.
- $L$ and $S$ are taken in the universe of $K$, as the docstring says; every finite extension of $K$ has a copy there, so this restricts nothing.
- The singular case: if the discriminant of $W$ is $0$, no equation has good reduction, and the proposition is false.

## What it says
If an elliptic curve $E$ over a nonarchimedean local field $K$ has potential good reduction, there is a finite extension $M$ of $K$ whose inertia acts trivially on the $\ell$-adic Tate module $T_\ell(E)$, for every prime $\ell$ different from the residue characteristic.

- `[Field K] [ValuativeRel K] [TopologicalSpace K] [IsNonarchimedeanLocalField K]`: $K$ is a nonarchimedean local field: a field with a valuation, given up to equivalence by a valuative relation, and the topology it defines, locally compact, with a nontrivial valuation.
- `[DecidableEq (AlgebraicClosure K)]`: equality in the algebraic closure $\bar K$ can be decided; a technical hypothesis.
- `(h : HasPotentialGoodReduction (↥(ValuativeRel.valuation K).integer) W)`: the Weierstrass equation $W$ over $K$, given implicitly, has potential good reduction with respect to the ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K = \{x : v(x) \le 1\}$: it acquires good reduction over some finite extension.
- The conclusion: there is a field $M$ with $K \subseteq M \subseteq \bar K$, finite-dimensional over $K$, such that for every prime $\ell$ that is nonzero in the residue field of $K$, every $\sigma$ in the inertia subgroup $I_K$ of $\operatorname{Gal}(\bar K/K)$ that fixes $M$ acts as the identity on $T_\ell(E)$, the Tate module of $W$ over $\bar K$: `(W.tateModuleGaloisRepresentation ℓ) σ = 1`.

This is one direction of the classical criterion for potential good reduction, that inertia acts on $T_\ell(E)$ through a finite quotient, in the precise form that the inertia subgroup of one finite extension, the same for every $\ell$, acts trivially.

## References and tests
- Silverman's proof of VII.7.3 — this theorem is its first step: over a finite extension where $E$ has good reduction, inertia acts trivially on $T_\ell(E)$ (VII.7.1, or VII.4.1), and the inertia of that extension is the set of inertia elements of $K$ that fix it.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `↑ℓ ≠ 0` casts $\ell$ into the residue field of $K$, as the source's `(ℓ : 𝓀[K]) ≠ 0` shows, so it says that $\ell$ is not the residue characteristic.
- `[inst : Fact (Nat.Prime ℓ)]` says that $\ell$ is prime, passed as a typeclass so that the $\ell$-adic integers can act on the Tate module.
- $M$ is chosen before $\ell$: one finite extension serves every $\ell$ at once.
- The Galois group is that of `AlgebraicClosure K` over $K$; every automorphism of a separable closure extends uniquely to it, so this is the absolute Galois group.
- `= 1` is the identity map of the Tate module, a module over the $\ell$-adic integers.
- `M.fixingSubgroup` is the subgroup of automorphisms fixing $M$ pointwise, the absolute Galois group of $M$; its intersection with $I_K$ is the inertia subgroup of $M$.
- No ellipticity is assumed: potential good reduction already forces the discriminant to be nonzero.

## What it says
If an elliptic curve $E$ over a nonarchimedean local field $K$ has potential good reduction, then for every prime $\ell$ different from the residue characteristic, inertia acts on the $\ell$-adic Tate module $T_\ell(E)$ through a finite quotient.

- `[Field K] [ValuativeRel K] [TopologicalSpace K] [IsNonarchimedeanLocalField K]`: $K$ is a nonarchimedean local field: a field with a valuation, given up to equivalence by a valuative relation, and the topology it defines, locally compact, with a nontrivial valuation.
- `[DecidableEq (AlgebraicClosure K)]`: equality in the algebraic closure $\bar K$ can be decided; a technical hypothesis.
- `(h : HasPotentialGoodReduction (↥(ValuativeRel.valuation K).integer) W)`: the Weierstrass equation $W$ over $K$, given implicitly, has potential good reduction with respect to the ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K = \{x : v(x) \le 1\}$.
- `(ℓ : ℕ)`: a natural number $\ell$.
- `[Fact (Nat.Prime ℓ)]`: $\ell$ is prime.
- `(hℓ : ↑ℓ ≠ 0)`: $\ell$ is nonzero in the residue field of $K$, that is, $\ell$ is not the residue characteristic $p$.
- The conclusion: the image of the inertia subgroup $I_K$ of $\operatorname{Gal}(\bar K/K)$ under the $\ell$-adic representation $\rho_\ell$ on $T_\ell(E)$, the Tate module of $W$ over $\bar K$, is a finite set.

A finite image of $I_K$ means that $\rho_\ell$ restricted to $I_K$ has a kernel of finite index, so that inertia acts through a finite quotient. This is the implication from potential good reduction in the classical criterion, as the docstring says.

## References and tests
- Silverman AEC VII.7.3 — the implication from potential good reduction, which this theorem states for each prime $\ell$ different from the residue characteristic.

No test is recorded for it.

## Lean subtleties
- `⇑(W.tateModuleGaloisRepresentation ℓ) '' ↑(TauCeti.inertiaSubgroup K)` is the image, `''`, of the inertia subgroup, seen as a set, under the representation, seen as a function from the Galois group to the endomorphisms of the Tate module; `.Finite` says that this image is a finite set.
- `hℓ : ↑ℓ ≠ 0` casts $\ell$ into the residue field of $K$, as the source's `(ℓ : 𝓀[K]) ≠ 0` shows. The hypothesis matters: for $\ell = p$ and good ordinary reduction, inertia acts on the $p$-adic Tate module through the cyclotomic character, whose image is infinite.
- Only the image of inertia is finite; the image of the whole Galois group is infinite in general.
- `[Fact (Nat.Prime ℓ)]` passes the primality of $\ell$ as a typeclass, so that the $\ell$-adic integers can act on the Tate module.
- The Galois group is that of `AlgebraicClosure K` over $K$, the absolute Galois group.
- No ellipticity is assumed: potential good reduction already forces the discriminant to be nonzero.

## What it says
A Weierstrass equation for an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ is reduced minimal when it is globally minimal over $\mathbb{Z}$ and its coefficients satisfy $a_1, a_3 \in \{0, 1\}$ and $a_2 \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$.

- `(W : WeierstrassCurve ℚ)`: a Weierstrass equation $y^2 + a_1xy + a_3y = x^3 + a_2x^2 + a_4x + a_6$ with rational coefficients.
- `[W.IsElliptic]`: its discriminant $\Delta$ is nonzero, so $W$ is an elliptic curve.
- The value: the conjunction of
  - `IsGlobalMinimal ℤ W`: $W$ is a minimal equation over $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ at every prime $p$, which makes its coefficients integers and $|\Delta|$ the least among the integral equations of the curve;
  - $a_1 = 0$ or $a_1 = 1$; $a_2 = -1$, $0$ or $1$; $a_3 = 0$ or $a_3 = 1$.

This is the reduced minimal model of the tables of elliptic curves over $\mathbb{Q}$, the normalisation of their coefficient vectors. The global minimal equations of a curve differ by changes of variables $x = u^2x' + r$, $y = u^3y' + su^2x' + t$ with $u = \pm 1$ and $r, s, t \in \mathbb{Z}$; the conditions on $a_1, a_2, a_3$ pin down one equation among them, as the third test proves.

## References and tests
- LeanBridge/LMFDB knowl — on the minimal Weierstrass equation over $\mathbb{Q}$, [`ec.q.minimal_weierstrass_equation`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.q.minimal_weierstrass_equation): the reduced minimal model condition that this definition spells out.
- `TauCeti.WorkedExamples.isReducedMinimal_curve11a2` — passes: $y^2 + y = x^3 - x^2 - 10x - 20$, the curve LMFDB 11.a2 (Cremona 11a1), is reduced minimal.
- `TauCeti.WorkedExamples.isReducedMinimal_curve37a1` — passes: $y^2 + y = x^3 - x$ is reduced minimal.
- `WeierstrassCurve.existsUnique_reducedMinimal` — passes: every elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ has exactly one reduced minimal equation among those obtained from it by changes of variables over $\mathbb{Q}$.

The two worked curves are tabulated equations, with $a_1 = 0$, $a_3 = 1$ and $a_2 = -1$ or $0$; the third test is the property that makes the normalisation a normal form.

## Lean subtleties
- The coefficient conditions are equalities in $\mathbb{Q}$; since a globally minimal equation is integral, they are conditions on integers.
- It is a property of a given equation and chooses nothing: the existence and uniqueness of the reduced minimal equation of a curve is the separate theorem in the third test.
- That theorem makes the equation unique, not the change of variables reaching it, which is unique only up to the automorphisms of the curve, such as $u = -1$.
- `[W.IsElliptic]` is a hypothesis carried as a typeclass, which Lean finds by itself.
- This is the long Weierstrass form, with $a_1, a_2, a_3$, not a short equation $y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B$.

## What it says
A Weierstrass equation $W$ for an elliptic curve over the fraction field $K$ of a Dedekind domain $O$ is semi-globally minimal when it is integral and minimal at every nonzero prime of $O$ except possibly one.

- `[CommRing O] [IsDedekindDomain O]`: $O$ is a Dedekind domain, such as the ring of integers of a number field.
- `[Field K] [Algebra O K] [IsFractionRing O K]`: $K$ is the fraction field of $O$.
- `(W : WeierstrassCurve K)`: a Weierstrass equation $W$ over $K$.
- `[W.IsElliptic]`: its discriminant is nonzero, so $W$ is an elliptic curve.
- The value: either
  - `IsGlobalMinimal O W`: $W$ is minimal over the localisation $O_v$ at every height-one prime $v$ of $O$; or
  - there is a height-one prime $v_0$ such that $W$ has coefficients in $O_{v_0}$ (`IsIntegral`), and $W$ is minimal over $O_v$ at every height-one prime $v \neq v_0$ (`IsMinimal`).

This is a semi-global minimal model: an integral equation minimal at every prime but at most one. Over a number field of class number greater than one, a curve need not have a globally minimal equation but always has a semi-globally minimal one; as the docstring says, that existence theorem is not proved here. The definition does not bound how far from minimal $W$ may be at $v_0$.

## References and tests
- LMFDB `ec.semi_global_minimal_model` — the semi-global minimal model, cited by the docstring as the source of this definition.
- LeanBridge — its blueprint copy of that knowl, [`ec.semi_global_minimal_model`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.semi_global_minimal_model): minimal except possibly at one prime, with a final sentence fixing the excess of the discriminant at the exceptional prime at exactly twelve, which is the sharp predicate `IsSharpSemiGlobalMinimalAt` rather than this one.
- `WeierstrassCurve.IsSharpSemiGlobalMinimalAt.isSemiGlobalMinimal` — passes: an equation that is sharply semi-globally minimal at a prime $v_0$ is semi-globally minimal.

The test places this definition below the sharp one, as the weaker of the two notions.

## Lean subtleties
- The first disjunct is needed when $O$ is a field, which Lean counts as a Dedekind domain: it has no nonzero primes, so the existential is false, while global minimality holds vacuously.
- Integrality at the primes $v \neq v_0$ is part of minimality there, so $W$ has coefficients in every $O_v$, hence in $O$.
- `HeightOneSpectrum O` is the type of nonzero prime ideals of $O$, and `Localization.AtPrime v.asIdeal` is the discrete valuation ring $O_v$.
- `IsMinimal` is phrased with Lean's multiplicative valuations: the valuation of $\Delta$ is maximal there, which is the least additive valuation.
- It is a property of one equation and asserts nothing about existence; $v_0$ is not part of the data.

## What it says
An elliptic curve over the fraction field $F$ of a Dedekind domain $O$ is semistable when, at every nonzero prime of $O$, a minimal equation for it does not have additive reduction; equivalently, its reduction is good or multiplicative everywhere.

- `[CommRing O] [IsDedekindDomain O]`: $O$ is a Dedekind domain, such as the ring of integers of a number field.
- `[Field F] [Algebra O F] [IsFractionRing O F]`: $F$ is the fraction field of $O$.
- `(W : WeierstrassCurve F)`: a Weierstrass equation $W$ over $F$.
- `[_hE : W.IsElliptic]`: its discriminant is nonzero, so $W$ is an elliptic curve.
- The value: for every height-one prime $v$ of $O$, a nonzero prime ideal, the minimal equation `W.minimal (Localization.AtPrime v.asIdeal)` of $W$ over the discrete valuation ring $O_v$ does not have additive reduction, `HasAdditiveReduction`, the bad reduction in which the reduced cubic has a cusp.

This is the usual notion of a semistable elliptic curve, as the docstring says: at every prime the reduction is good or multiplicative. For a curve over a number field, with $O$ its ring of integers, there is no condition at the infinite places, as in the usual definition.

## References and tests
- LeanBridge/LMFDB knowl — on semistable curves, [`ec.semistable`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.semistable): multiplicative reduction at every bad prime, the notion this definition states over any Dedekind domain.
- `TauCeti.WorkedExamples.isSemistable_curve11a1` — passes: the curve 11.a1 over $\mathbb{Q}$, whose only bad reduction is multiplicative, is semistable.
- `TauCeti.WorkedExamples.not_isSemistable_curve27a4` — passes: the curve 27.a4 over $\mathbb{Q}$, with additive reduction of Kodaira type II at $3$, is not semistable.

The two tests take one curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ of each kind, one semistable and one with additive reduction, and the predicate decides both as the tables do.

## Lean subtleties
- `HeightOneSpectrum O` is the type of nonzero prime ideals of $O$, and `Localization.AtPrime v.asIdeal` is the discrete valuation ring $O_v$.
- A minimal equation is computed at each prime before the reduction type is read, so the predicate does not depend on the equation given; the docstring records that it depends only on the isomorphism class of $W$ over $F$, by `isSemistable_smul`.
- `[_hE : W.IsElliptic]` is not used by the definition, as the underscore in its name records; it keeps out singular cubics, which have no reduction type.
- If $O$ is a field, which Lean counts as a Dedekind domain, it has no nonzero primes, and every elliptic curve over $F$ is semistable.
- Lean's valuations are multiplicative: the reduction types are phrased with valuations less than or equal to $1$, where additively one would say positive or zero.

## What it says
The abc quality of an elliptic curve $E$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ with $j$-invariant $j \neq 0, 1728$: write $j/1728 = a/c$ in lowest terms and $b = c - a$; the quality of the triple $(a, b, c)$ is $\log \max(|a|, |b|, |c|) / \log \operatorname{rad}(abc)$.

- `(E : WeierstrassCurve ℚ)`: a Weierstrass equation $E$ with rational coefficients.
- `[E.IsElliptic]`: its discriminant is nonzero, so $E$ is an elliptic curve with a $j$-invariant `E.j`.
- `(_h : E.j ≠ 0 ∧ E.j ≠ 1728)`: $j$ is neither $0$ nor $1728$.
- The value: with $a$ the numerator and $c > 0$ the denominator of $j/1728$ in lowest terms, and $b = c - a$, the real number $\log \max(|a|, |b|, |c|) / \log \operatorname{rad}(|abc|)$, where $\operatorname{rad}(n)$ is the product of the distinct primes dividing $n$.

Since $a/c = j/1728$ and $b/c = (1728 - j)/1728$, the relation $a + b = c$ is the identity $j/1728 + (1728 - j)/1728 = 1$ cleared of denominators, and $a, b, c$ are pairwise coprime. The value is the usual quality of this abc triple, with absolute values since $a$ and $b$ may be negative. The hypothesis on $j$ says exactly that $a \neq 0$ and $b \neq 0$.

## References and tests
- LeanBridge/LMFDB knowl — on the abc quality of an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$, [`ec.q.abc_quality`](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.q.abc_quality): the quality formula this definition implements, with the two cases $j = 0$ and $j = 1728$ left undefined.
- `WeierstrassCurve.abcQuality_eq_of_j_div_eq` — passes: for any coprime integers $a, c$ with $j/1728 = a/c$ and $b = c - a$, the quality is the formula computed from $a, b, c$.
- `WeierstrassCurve.abcQuality_pos` — passes: the quality is strictly positive.

The first test shows that the value does not depend on the representative of $j/1728$, a negative denominator included; the second, that the denominator $\log \operatorname{rad}(abc)$ is positive, so no division by zero occurs.

## Lean subtleties
- `(E.j / 1728).num` and `.den` are the numerator and denominator that Lean stores for a rational number: in lowest terms, with a positive denominator.
- `natAbs` is the absolute value as a natural number, so the signs of $a$ and $b$ do not affect the value.
- `radical` is the product of the distinct prime factors, without multiplicity.
- `Real.log` is the natural logarithm; the ratio does not depend on the base. Lean sets `Real.log 0 = 0` and $x/0 = 0$: under the hypothesis on $j$ the radical is at least $2$, and without it the value would be $0$.
- The hypothesis `_h` is not used in the computation, as the underscore in its name records; it only restricts the domain.
- The value depends on $j$ alone, so it is the same for all curves with the same $j$-invariant, twists included.

## What it says
For an elliptic curve $W$ over the fraction field $K$ of a discrete valuation ring $R$ with perfect residue field, the natural number $v(\Delta_{\min}) - m + 1$, where $v(\Delta_{\min})$ is the valuation of the minimal discriminant of $W$ and $m$ is the component count of the reduction symbol at which Tate's algorithm stops on a minimal equation of $W$.

- `[CommRing R] [IsDomain R] [IsDiscreteValuationRing R]`: $R$ is a discrete valuation ring, a local principal ideal domain that is not a field; $v$ is its normalised valuation.
- `[Field K] [Algebra R K] [IsFractionRing R K]`: $K$ is a field with a map from $R$ that makes it the fraction field of $R$.
- `[PerfectField (IsLocalRing.ResidueField R)]`: the residue field of $R$ is perfect.
- `(W : WeierstrassCurve K)`: a Weierstrass equation $Y^2 + a_1XY + a_3Y = X^3 + a_2X^2 + a_4X + a_6$ with $a_i \in K$.
- `[W.IsElliptic]`: its discriminant is a unit of $K$, so $W$ is an elliptic curve.
- The value: `localMinimalDiscriminantValuation` gives $v(\Delta_{\min})$, `reductionSymbol` the reduction symbol, and `ReductionSymbol.algorithmicOggExponent` forms the integer $v(\Delta_{\min}) - m + 1$, which `Int.toNat` turns into a natural number.

Ogg's formula $v(\Delta_{\min}) = f + m - 1$ links the exponent $f$ of the conductor to the minimal discriminant and to the number $m$ of components of the special fibre of the minimal regular model. This definition reads $f$ off that formula from the output of Tate's algorithm, hence "algorithmic". As the docstring says, it is $0$ at good reduction, $1$ at multiplicative reduction and at least $2$ at additive reduction, as the conductor exponent is. Its agreement with a conductor defined through ramification is not part of this declaration.

## References and tests
- Blueprint `ec.q.conductor` — the conductor of an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$, whose local exponents this definition computes by Ogg's formula.
- `WeierstrassCurve.natCast_algorithmicOggExponent` — cast to $\mathbb{Z}$, the value is the integer $v(\Delta_{\min}) - m + 1$ itself: that integer is never negative, so nothing is cut off.
- `WeierstrassCurve.algorithmicOggExponent_eq_zero_iff` — the value is $0$ exactly when the minimal model has good reduction.
- `WeierstrassCurve.algorithmicOggExponent_eq_one_iff` — the value is $1$ exactly when the minimal model has multiplicative reduction.

The last two settle the two cases where the conductor exponent is known by hand, and together they leave the values $\geq 2$ to additive reduction, as the docstring says.

## Lean subtleties
- `Int.toNat` sends every negative integer to $0$; the first test shows that the integer it is applied to here is never negative, so no junk value arises.
- The hypotheses in square brackets are typeclasses, which Lean finds by itself. `[W.IsElliptic]` asks that the discriminant be a unit of $K$, which in a field means nonzero.
- The valuation is normalised, with value $1$ at a uniformiser: `localMinimalDiscriminantValuation` is the exponent of the maximal ideal of $R$ in the minimal discriminant.
- $R$ need not be complete; its residue field must be perfect, the standing hypothesis of Tate's algorithm.
- `Type u_1` and `Type u_2` say that $R$ and $K$ are types, Lean's sets; the universe levels do not affect the mathematics.

## What it says
For an elliptic curve $E$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ whose conductor $N$ exceeds $1$, the Szpiro ratio $\sigma_E = \log|\Delta_{\min}| / \log N$, where $\Delta_{\min}$ is the minimal discriminant of $E$.

- `(E : WeierstrassCurve ℚ)`: a Weierstrass equation $y^2 + a_1xy + a_3y = x^3 + a_2x^2 + a_4x + a_6$ with rational coefficients.
- `[E.IsElliptic]`: its discriminant is nonzero, so $E$ is an elliptic curve.
- `(_h : 1 < Ideal.absNorm (algorithmicConductor ℤ E))`: the conductor is greater than $1$. Here `algorithmicConductor ℤ E` is the conductor ideal $\prod_p p^{f_p}$ of $\mathbb{Z}$, its exponents $f_p$ computed by Tate's algorithm, and `Ideal.absNorm` of an ideal $I$ of $\mathbb{Z}$ is the size of $\mathbb{Z}/I$, which is $|n|$ for $I = (n)$; so this norm is the conductor $N$.
- The value: the real number $\log|\Delta_{\min}| / \log N$, where $|\Delta_{\min}|$ is the norm of `minimalDiscriminantIdeal ℤ E`, the ideal $\prod_p p^{v_p(\Delta_{\min})}$ of $\mathbb{Z}$, which is generated by the minimal discriminant.

This is the Szpiro ratio of the literature, the quantity in Szpiro's conjecture $|\Delta_{\min}| \ll_\varepsilon N^{6+\varepsilon}$. It is the ordinary ratio, with the minimal discriminant in the numerator; the modified Szpiro ratio, with numerator $\log\max(|c_4|^3, c_6^2)$, is a different quantity.

## References and tests
- [the LeanBridge/LMFDB knowl](https://github.com/CBirkbeck/LeanBridge/blob/6010bdde38e723b4ace379f4006d2adb4c250ba4/blueprint/src/knowls/ec/ec.q.szpiro_ratio) — the LMFDB's entry on the Szpiro ratio of an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$.
- `WeierstrassCurve.rpow_algorithmicSzpiroRatio` — under the same hypothesis, $N^{\sigma_E} = |\Delta_{\min}|$.
- `WeierstrassCurve.algorithmicSzpiroRatio_smul` — the ratio is unchanged by a change of variables over $\mathbb{Q}$.

The first test inverts the definition: raising $N$ to the ratio gives back $|\Delta_{\min}|$, so both logarithms are the true ones and no junk value enters. The second shows that the ratio depends only on the curve, not on the equation chosen for it, as the Szpiro ratio does.

## Lean subtleties
- Lean's division and logarithm are total: $x/0 = 0$, $\log 0 = 0$, and $\log 1 = 0$, so a curve with $N = 1$ would get the ratio $0$. The hypothesis `_h` excludes this. It is no real restriction: no elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ has good reduction at every prime, so its conductor is never $1$.
- `Ideal.absNorm` has the junk value $0$ at the zero ideal; neither ideal here is zero, since the discriminant of an elliptic curve is nonzero.
- The norms are natural numbers, cast to real numbers before the logarithm is taken. `Real.log` is the natural logarithm; the base cancels in the ratio.
- `_h` is a proof, not a number: the value does not depend on it, and its leading underscore records that the formula does not use it.
- "Algorithmic" in the name: the conductor exponents are those Tate's algorithm computes through Ogg's formula, not ones read off the Galois action on the Tate module.

## What it says

## What it says
For a Weierstrass equation over $\mathbb{R}$, the integral $\int_{\{\Psi(x) > 0\}} dx/\sqrt{\Psi(x)}$, a value in $[0, \infty]$, where $\Psi(x) = 4x^3 + b_2x^2 + 2b_4x + b_6$; for an elliptic curve it is half the real period.

- `(W : WeierstrassCurve ℝ)`: a Weierstrass equation $y^2 + a_1xy + a_3y = x^3 + a_2x^2 + a_4x + a_6$ with real coefficients; it need not be elliptic.
- The value: the Lebesgue integral, over the set of real $x$ with $\Psi(x) > 0$, of $1/\sqrt{\Psi(x)}$, where $\Psi$ is `W.Ψ₂Sq`, with $b_2 = a_1^2 + 4a_2$, $b_4 = 2a_4 + a_1a_3$ and $b_6 = a_3^2 + 4a_6$. On the curve, $\Psi(x) = (2y + a_1x + a_3)^2$.

The real period is $\Omega = \int_{E(\mathbb{R})} |\omega|$ for the invariant differential $\omega = dx/(2y + a_1x + a_3)$. Above each $x$ with $\Psi(x) > 0$ lie exactly two real points, and each contributes $dx/\sqrt{\Psi(x)}$, so $\Omega$ is twice this integral, whether $E(\mathbb{R})$ has one component or two. The docstring records that `WeierstrassCurve.realPeriod` is twice this value whenever it is finite (`WeierstrassCurve.ofReal_realPeriod`).

## What it says
The Shafarevich–Tate group $\text{Ш}(E/K)$ of a Weierstrass curve $E$ over a number field $K$: the classes in $H^1(G_K, E(K^s))$ whose restriction to the completion $K_v$ vanishes at every place $v$ of $K$, finite and infinite.

- The value: a subgroup of $H^1(G_K, E(K^s))$, the first continuous cohomology group of the absolute Galois group $G_K$, with coefficients in the points of $W$ over a separable closure $K^s$. Then every element of the inertia group of $K$ that fixes $\iota(L)$ acts trivially on the $\ell$-adic Tate module of $W$, for every prime $\ell$ different from the residue characteristic of $K$.

- `[Field K] [ValuativeRel K] [TopologicalSpace K] [IsNonarchimedeanLocalField K]`: $K$, with its valuation and its topology, is a nonarchimedean local field, such as a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}_p$ or $\mathbb{F}_q((t))$. $W$ is a Weierstrass equation over $K$.
- `[Field L] [ValuativeRel L] [TopologicalSpace L] [IsNonarchimedeanLocalField L]`: $L$ is a nonarchimedean local field too.
- `[Algebra K L] [ValuativeExtension K L] [FiniteDimensional K L]`: $L$ is a finite extension of $K$ whose valuation restricts to that of $K$.
- `(ι : L →ₐ[K] AlgebraicClosure K)`: an embedding $\iota$ of $L$ over $K$ into an algebraic closure $\bar K$.
- `(C : VariableChange L)`: a change of Weierstrass variables over $L$.
- `[IsIntegral (↥(ValuativeRel.valuation L).integer) (C • W.baseChange L)]`: after the change $C$, the equation of $W$ over $L$ has coefficients in the valuation ring $\mathcal O_L$.
- `[(integralModel (↥(ValuativeRel.valuation L).integer) (C • W.baseChange L)).IsElliptic]`: that equation, read over $\mathcal O_L$, has discriminant a unit of $\mathcal O_L$: $W$ has good reduction over $L$.
- `[DecidableEq (AlgebraicClosure K)]`: a procedure deciding equality in $\bar K$, which the group law on points uses.
- `[Fact (Nat.Prime ℓ)]`: $\ell$ is prime.
- `(hℓ : ↑ℓ ≠ 0)`: $\ell$ is nonzero in the residue field of $K$, that is $\ell$ is not the residue characteristic.
- `(hσ : σ ∈ TauCeti.inertiaSubgroup K)`: $\sigma \in \mathrm{Gal}(\bar K/K)$ lies in the inertia group $I_K$.
- `(hσL : σ ∈ ι.fieldRange.fixingSubgroup)`: $\sigma$ fixes $\iota(L)$ pointwise.
- The conclusion: $\sigma$ acts as the identity on $T_\ell = \varprojlim_n W(\bar K)[\ell^n]$.

The elements of $I_K$ fixing $\iota(L)$ form the inertia group of $L$, so this is the classical fact that the Tate module of a curve with good reduction is unramified, applied over $L$: the form needed for potentially good reduction.

## What it says
The Galois action on $N$-torsion: an $F$-automorphism $\sigma$ of an extension $K$ permutes the points of a Weierstrass curve $W$ over $K$ by acting on their coordinates, and restricted to the subgroup $W(K)[N]$ of points killed by $N$ this gives a group homomorphism from $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ to the automorphisms of $W(K)[N]$.

- `[Field F] [Field K]`: $F$ and $K$ are fields.
- `[DecidableEq K]`: a procedure deciding equality in $K$, which the group law on the points over $K$ uses.
- `[Algebra F K]`: $K$ is an extension of $F$.
- `(W : WeierstrassCurve F)`: a Weierstrass equation $Y^2 + a_1XY + a_3Y = X^3 + a_2X^2 + a_4X + a_6$ with $a_i \in F$.
- `(N : ℤ)`: an integer $N$.

The value is a group homomorphism from $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$, the group of $F$-automorphisms of $K$, to the group of automorphisms of the abelian group $W(K)[N] = \{P \in W(K) : NP = 0\}$. To $\sigma$ it assigns the restriction to $W(K)[N]$ of the automorphism $P \mapsto \sigma(P)$ of $W(K)$, which applies $\sigma$ to the coordinates and carries $N$-torsion to $N$-torsion. Since $\sigma\tau$ is $\tau$ followed by $\sigma$, $\sigma\tau$ acts as $\sigma$ after $\tau$: a left action.

When $K$ is a separable closure of $F$, $W$ is an elliptic curve and $N$ is prime to the characteristic, $W(K)[N]$ is free of rank $2$ over $\mathbb{Z}/N$ and this is the mod-$N$ Galois representation, without a basis.

## What it says
For an elliptic curve given by a Weierstrass equation $W$ with coefficients in a Dedekind domain $O$, this is the class $[\mathfrak J_W]$ in the ideal class group of $O$ of the ideal $\mathfrak J_W$ that measures the excess of the discriminant of $W$ over the minimal discriminant: $(\Delta_W) = \mathfrak D_{\min} \mathfrak J_W^{12}$.

- `[CommRing O] [IsDedekindDomain O]`: $O$ is a Dedekind domain, such as the ring of integers of a number field.
- `[Field K] [Algebra O K] [IsFractionRing O K]`: $K$ is a field together with a map from $O$ that makes $K$ the field of fractions of $O$.
- `(W : WeierstrassCurve O)`: a Weierstrass equation $Y^2 + a_1XY + a_3Y = X^3 + a_2X^2 + a_4X + a_6$ with $a_i \in O$, an integral equation.
- `[(W.baseChange K).IsElliptic]`: read over $K$, $W$ is an elliptic curve: its discriminant $\Delta_W$ is nonzero.

The value lies in `ClassGroup O`, the invertible fractional ideals of $O$ modulo the principal ones. At each nonzero prime $\mathfrak p$ of $O$, the ideal $\mathfrak J_W$ has exponent $(v_{\mathfrak p}(\Delta_W) - v_{\mathfrak p}(\Delta_{\min,\mathfrak p}))/12$, where $\Delta_{\min,\mathfrak p}$ is the discriminant of a minimal equation at $\mathfrak p$. This exponent is a natural number, since $W$ is integral and a change of variables multiplies the discriminant by a twelfth power. The definition makes $W$, read over $K$, an integral equation over $O$, and takes the defect class of that.

This is the obstruction to a global minimal model: a change of variables over $K$ changes $\mathfrak J_W$ by a principal ideal, so the class belongs to the curve. It is the inverse of the Weierstrass class in the orientation of Silverman VIII.8, and is trivial exactly when that class is.

## What it says
Over a regular ring $R$, every module $M$ has projective dimension at most the Krull dimension of $R$: $\operatorname{pd}_R M \le \dim R$.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring.
- `[IsRegularRing R]`: $R$ is regular: noetherian, and its localization at every prime ideal is a regular local ring.
- `[Small.{v, u} R]`: $R$ is in bijection with a type in the universe `v` in which the modules live, a technical condition that does not restrict the mathematics.
- `(M : ModuleCat R)`: an $R$-module $M$, an object of the category of $R$-modules; it need not be finitely generated.
- The conclusion: `CategoryTheory.projectiveDimension M`, the projective dimension of $M$ in that abelian category (the least length of a projective resolution), is at most `ringKrullDim R`, the supremum of the lengths of chains of prime ideals of $R$.

This is the bound that makes the global dimension of a regular ring at most its Krull dimension, the hard half of Serre's theorem that the two are equal, in the form for all modules, with no finiteness hypothesis on $M$ or on $\dim R$.

## What it says
Serre's theorem, in one direction: a noetherian local ring whose residue field has finite projective dimension is a regular local ring.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring.
- `[IsLocalRing R]`: $R$ is local, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$; in particular $R \neq 0$.
- `[IsNoetherianRing R]`: $R$ is noetherian.
- `[Small.{v, u} R]`: $R$ is in bijection with a type in the universe `v` in which the modules live, a technical condition that does not restrict the mathematics.
- `(n : ℕ)`: a natural number $n$.
- `[CategoryTheory.HasProjectiveDimensionLE (↧(Shrink.{v, u} (R ⧸ IsLocalRing.maximalIdeal R))) n]`: the residue field $k = R/\mathfrak m$, as an $R$-module, has projective dimension at most $n$, that is $\operatorname{Ext}^i_R(k, Y) = 0$ for every $R$-module $Y$ and every $i \ge n + 1$.
- The conclusion: `IsRegularLocalRing R`, $R$ is a regular local ring: its maximal ideal is generated by $\dim R$ elements.

This is the hard direction of Serre's characterisation of regular local rings: $R$ is regular if and only if $k$ has finite projective dimension, if and only if $R$ has finite global dimension. Here the hypothesis is the weakest of the three, finiteness for the residue field alone.

## What it says
The Cohen structure theorem with the fewest variables. A complete local ring $R$ that contains a field and whose maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ is finitely generated has a coefficient field, and is a quotient of the power series ring over its residue field $\kappa$ in $d$ variables, $d$ the least number of generators of $\mathfrak m$. The surjection is the coefficient field on constants and sends the variables to generators of $\mathfrak m$.

- `[Field k]`: $k$ is a field.
- `[CommRing R] [IsLocalRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative local ring, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ and residue field $\kappa = R/\mathfrak m$.
- `[Algebra k R]`: $R$ is a $k$-algebra; as $R \neq 0$, it contains a copy of the field $k$, so it has equal characteristic.
- `[IsAdicComplete (IsLocalRing.maximalIdeal R) R]`: $R$ is $\mathfrak m$-adically complete: separated, and every $\mathfrak m$-adic Cauchy sequence converges.
- `(hfg : (IsLocalRing.maximalIdeal R).FG)`: $\mathfrak m$ is finitely generated.
- The conclusion: there is a ring map $s : \kappa \to R$ with $s(a) \equiv a \bmod \mathfrak m$ for all $a$, a coefficient field. With $d$ = `Submodule.spanFinrank (IsLocalRing.maximalIdeal R)`, the least size of a generating set of $\mathfrak m$, there is moreover a surjective ring map $\varphi : \kappa[[X_0, \dots, X_{d-1}]] \to R$ that agrees with $s$ on constants and sends $X_0, \dots, X_{d-1}$ to elements that generate $\mathfrak m$.

The classical theorem assumes $R$ noetherian. Here only $\mathfrak m$ is assumed finitely generated, which for a complete local ring already makes it noetherian, so this is the classical statement, with the number of variables the embedding dimension $\dim_\kappa \mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$, as small as possible.

## What it says
For a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ over a nonarchimedean local field $E$, a subgroup $K$ of $\mathrm{GL}(V)$ has compact closure if and only if it stabilises a lattice: an $\mathcal O_E$-submodule $L$ that is finitely generated and spans $V$, with $kL \subseteq L$ for every $k \in K$.

- `[Field E] [ValuativeRel E] [TopologicalSpace E] [IsNonarchimedeanLocalField E]`: $E$, with its valuation and its topology, is a nonarchimedean local field, such as a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}_p$ or $\mathbb{F}_q((t))$.
- `[AddCommGroup V] [Module E V]`: $V$ is a vector space over $E$.
- `[Module (↥(ValuativeRel.valuation E).integer) V] [IsScalarTower (↥(ValuativeRel.valuation E).integer) E V]`: $V$ is also a module over the ring of integers $\mathcal O_E$ of $E$, the elements of valuation at most $1$, by restricting scalars from $E$.
- `[TopologicalSpace V] [IsModuleTopology E V]`: $V$ carries its natural topology as a module over $E$, that of $E^n$ under any basis.
- `[FiniteDimensional E V]`: $V$ is finite-dimensional over $E$.
- `(K : Subgroup (V ≃ₗ[E] V))`: a subgroup $K$ of the group $\mathrm{GL}(V)$ of invertible $E$-linear maps of $V$.
- The conclusion: the closure of $K$ in $\mathrm{GL}(V)$ is compact if and only if there is an $\mathcal O_E$-submodule $L$ of $V$ that is a lattice (`Submodule.IsLattice E L`: finitely generated, and spanning $V$ over $E$) such that $k(x) \in L$ for all $k \in K$ and $x \in L$.

This is the classical criterion behind the fact that a continuous representation of a compact group over a local field preserves a lattice, and so can be conjugated into $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal O_E)$.
