Let $P$ be a property of finite-type commutative Hopf algebras over $R$ that is invariant under isomorphism. If $I$ is a minimal Hopf ideal of $K$ among those $J$ with $K/J$ satisfying $P$, and $e : H \to K$ is an isomorphism, then the inverse image $e^{-1}(I)$ is a minimal Hopf ideal of $H$ among those $J$ with $H/J$ satisfying $P$.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring, with a $1$; $H$ and $K$ are objects of `FiniteTypeCommHopfAlgCat R`, commutative $R$-Hopf algebras of finite type.

- `[P.IsClosedUnderIsomorphisms]`: if $A$ satisfies $P$ and $B \cong A$, then $B$ satisfies $P$.
- `(I : HopfIdeal R ↑K.obj)`: a Hopf ideal $I$ of $K$, an ideal that is also a coideal and is stable under the antipode, so that $K/I$ is again a Hopf algebra.
- `(hI : Minimal (fun (J : HopfIdeal R ↑K.obj) => P (K.quotient J)) I)`: $K/I$ satisfies $P$, and no Hopf ideal $J \subsetneq I$ has $K/J$ satisfying $P$.

## What it says
A point representation of the affine group $G$ represented by a commutative Hopf algebra $H$, on an $R$-module $V$. It is a family of group homomorphisms $G(A) \to \mathrm{GL}_A(A \otimes_R V)$, one for each commutative $R$-algebra $A$, natural in $A$.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring with a $1$, the base ring.
- `[CommRing H] [HopfAlgebra R H]`: $H$ is a commutative Hopf algebra over $R$, with comultiplication, counit and antipode. Its $A$-points, the $R$-algebra homomorphisms $H \to A$, form a group $G(A)$ under the convolution product.
- `[AddCommMonoid V] [Module R V]`: $V$ is an $R$-module.

Its value is the type of natural transformations from `pointsFunctor` to `GeneralLinear.scalarExtensionAutomorphismsFunctor`. The first is the functor $A \mapsto G(A)$. The second is the functor $A \mapsto \mathrm{GL}_A(A \otimes_R V)$ of $A$-linear automorphisms of $A \otimes_R V$. Both are functors from commutative $R$-algebras to groups. An element $\Theta$ gives a group homomorphism $\Theta_A : G(A) \to \mathrm{GL}_A(A \otimes_R V)$ for each $A$. For every algebra homomorphism $\varphi : A \to B$ and every $A$-point $x$, extending $\Theta_A(x)$ along $\varphi$ gives $\Theta_B(\varphi \circ x)$.

This is the standard definition of a linear representation of an affine group as a homomorphism of group functors $G \to \mathrm{GL}_V$. It is the definition of the recorded reference, with the tensor factors in the other order. It is stated over any commutative ring $R$, with no finiteness or freeness assumption on $V$.

- `≤` on Hopf ideals is containment, and it reverses the order of subgroups: the result goes up in ideals and down in subgroups.
- Every Hopf ideal lies in the kernel of the counit, since $\varepsilon(I) = 0$; that kernel, the ideal of the trivial subgroup, is where the order ends.

## What it says
For a commutative Hopf algebra $H$ over a commutative semiring $R$, the coordinate ring of $G = \operatorname{Spec} H$, and a Hopf ideal $I$ of $H$, which cuts out the closed subgroup $N = V(I)$, `I.IsNormal` says that $N$ is normal in $G$: the ideal generated by $c(I)$ lies in $H \otimes I$, where $c : H \to H \otimes_R H$ is the coordinate map of conjugation $(g, y) \mapsto gyg^{-1}$, with $g$ in the first factor.

- `[CommSemiring R]`: $R$ is a commutative semiring, the base.
- `[CommSemiring H] [HopfAlgebra R H]`: $H$ is a commutative Hopf algebra over $R$.
- `(I : HopfIdeal R H)`: a Hopf ideal of $H$, a two-sided ideal with $\Delta(I) \subseteq I \otimes H + H \otimes I$, $\varepsilon(I) = 0$ and $S(I) \subseteq I$.
- The conclusion: a proposition (`Prop`).
- The value: `Ideal.map` of `I.toIdeal` along the ring map underlying `HopfAlgebra.conjugationAlgHom`, the ideal of $H \otimes_R H$ generated by $c(I)$, is contained (`≤`) in `Ideal.rightTensorIdeal` of `I.toIdeal`, the ideal generated by the $1 \otimes i$ with $i \in I$, which stands for $H \otimes I$.

$H \otimes I$ is the ideal of $G \times N$, with $N$ in the second factor, the one conjugated. So the condition says that conjugation $G \times N \to G$ lands in $N$: $gng^{-1}$ is a point of $N$ for all points $g$ of $G$ and $n$ of $N$, with values in any $R$-algebra. This is the standard notion of a normal subgroup scheme, written in coordinate rings; it is stated over commutative semirings, which contain the usual commutative rings.

## References and tests
- [Milne, §1.j](https://www.jmilne.org/math/Books/iAG2022.pdf#page=42) — a subgroup preserved by conjugation.
- `TauCeti.CommHopfAlgCat.isNormal_iff_quotientPointsSubgroup_normal` — over a commutative ring $R$, $I$ is normal exactly when, for every commutative $R$-algebra $A$, the points $N(A)$ form a normal subgroup of $G(A)$.
- `TauCeti.HopfIdeal.isNormal_bot` — the zero Hopf ideal, whose subgroup is all of $G$, is normal.

The first test is the equivalence with the definition by points, normality in every group $G(A)$, which is the usual one; the second is the degenerate case of the whole group.

## What it says
For a commutative Hopf algebra $H$ over a commutative ring $R$, the coordinate ring of $G = \operatorname{Spec} H$, a commutative $R$-algebra $B$ and a normal Hopf ideal $I$, which cuts out the normal subgroup $N = V(I)$, the adjoint action of any $B$-point $g$ of $G$ carries tangent vectors of $N$ with values in $B$ to tangent vectors of $N$: the Lie algebra of a normal subgroup is stable under the adjoint action.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring, the base.
- `[CommRing H] [HopfAlgebra R H]`: $H$ is a commutative Hopf algebra over $R$.
- `[CommRing B] [Algebra R B]`: $B$ is a commutative $R$-algebra, where points and tangent vectors take their values.
- `(hI : I.IsNormal)`: the Hopf ideal $I$ (implicit) is normal, $c(I) \subseteq H \otimes I$ for the coordinate map $c$ of conjugation: conjugation by points of $G$ preserves $N$.
- `(g : WithConv (H →ₐ[R] Bialgebra.CounitAlgebra R H B))`: an $R$-algebra map $g : H \to B$, a $B$-point of $G$, in `WithConv`, where points multiply by convolution.
- `(hd : d ∈ I.lieSubalgebra)`: $d$ (implicit) is a tangent vector of $G$ at the identity with values in $B$, an $R$-linear $d : H \to B$ with $d(xy) = \varepsilon(x)d(y) + \varepsilon(y)d(x)$, and it lies in the Lie subalgebra cut out by $I$, the tangent vectors of $N$.
- The conclusion: `Derivation.adDerivation B g d`, the adjoint action $\mathrm{Ad}(g)d = g * d * g^{-1}$ in convolution, the differential of conjugation by $g$, lies in `I.lieSubalgebra` again.

Conjugation by $g$ maps $N$ into itself, so its differential at the identity maps the Lie algebra of $N$ into itself: this is the standard fact, stated here for points with values in any commutative $R$-algebra and with no smoothness assumed.

## References and tests
- [Milne, 10.20–10.23](https://www.jmilne.org/math/Books/iAG2022.pdf#page=203) — the adjoint action of a group on its Lie algebra, the differential of conjugation.
- `Derivation.snd_conjugate_tangentPoint` — conjugating the tangent point $1 + \delta d$ over the dual numbers $B[\delta]$, $\delta^2 = 0$, by $g$ gives a point whose $\delta$-coefficient is $\mathrm{Ad}(g)d$.

The test ties `Derivation.adDerivation` to conjugation of points: $\mathrm{Ad}(g)d$ is the first-order part of $g(1 + \delta d)g^{-1}$, which normality keeps in $N$.

- `[CommRing R]`, `[CommRing H]`, `[HopfAlgebra R H]`, `[CommRing B]` and `[Algebra R B]` are hypotheses carried as typeclasses: Lean finds these structures by itself. `u_1`, `u_2` and `u_3` are universe levels, which do not affect the mathematics.
- `Bialgebra.CounitAlgebra R H B` is a type synonym for $B$, made an $H$-algebra through the counit followed by $R \to B$; derivations into it are the tangent vectors at the identity with values in $B$, and $R$-algebra maps into it are simply the $B$-points of $G$.
- `WithConv` is a type synonym in which `*` is convolution and `⁻¹` the convolution inverse, the group law of $G(B)$.
- $B$ is any commutative $R$-algebra, non-reduced ones such as dual numbers included.
- `I.lieSubalgebra` is a Lie subalgebra over $B$ of the tangent Lie algebra of $G$ with values in $B$.

## What it says
For a commutative Hopf algebra $H$ over a commutative ring $R$, the coordinate ring of $G = \operatorname{Spec} H$, a normal Hopf ideal $I$, which cuts out the normal subgroup $N = V(I)$, and a coinvariant $h$ of $I$, a function on $G$ invariant under right translation by $N$, the antipode $S(h)$ is again a coinvariant.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring, the base.
- `(hI : I.IsNormal)`: $I$ is normal, $c(I) \subseteq H \otimes I$ for the coordinate map $c$ of conjugation: conjugation preserves $N$. Here $H$, implicit, ranges over `CommHopfAlgCat R`, the commutative Hopf algebras over $R$, $I$ over the Hopf ideals of $H$, and $h$ over the elements of $H$.
- `(hh : h ∈ I.coinvariants)`: $h$ is a coinvariant, $(\mathrm{id} \otimes \pi)(\Delta h) = h \otimes 1$ with $\pi : H \to H/I$ the quotient map; on points, $h(gn) = h(g)$ for all points $g$ of $G$ and $n$ of $N$.
- The conclusion: `(HopfAlgebraStruct.antipode R) h`, the antipode $S(h)$, the function $g \mapsto h(g^{-1})$, lies in `I.coinvariants` too.

On points, $S(h)(gn) = h((gn)^{-1}) = h(g^{-1} \cdot g n^{-1} g^{-1}) = h(g^{-1})$, since $g n^{-1} g^{-1}$ is a point of $N$ by normality, as the docstring explains. This is one of the steps showing that the functions invariant under a normal subgroup form a Hopf subalgebra, the coordinate ring of $G/N$. Normality is what makes it hold: for $N$ not normal, $S$ turns right $N$-invariant functions into left $N$-invariant ones.

## References and tests
- [Milne, 3.3–3.5](https://www.jmilne.org/math/Books/iAG2022.pdf#page=76) — the antipode as the coordinate map of inversion $g \mapsto g^{-1}$.
- `TauCeti.HopfIdeal.IsNormal.isHopfSubalgebra_coinvariants` — for a normal $I$, with $H$ flat over $R$ and $H$ modulo the coinvariants flat too, the coinvariants form a Hopf subalgebra of $H$.

The test is the result this closure serves: a Hopf subalgebra must be stable under the antipode. Its flatness hypotheses are not needed for the closure stated here.

## What it says
For a commutative Hopf algebra $H$ over a commutative ring $R$, the coordinate ring of $G = \operatorname{Spec} H$, and a normal Hopf ideal $I$, which cuts out the normal subgroup $N = V(I)$, with $H$ and $H/B$ flat over $R$, where $B$ is the subalgebra of coinvariants of $I$, this is $B$ as a subcoalgebra of $H$: the functions on $G$ invariant under right translation by $N$ satisfy $\Delta(B) \subseteq B \otimes B$.

- `[CommRing R]`: $R$ is a commutative ring, the base. Here $H$, implicit, ranges over `CommHopfAlgCat R`, the commutative Hopf algebras over $R$, and $I$ over the Hopf ideals of $H$.
- `[Module.Flat R ↑H]`: $H$ is a flat $R$-module.
- `[Module.Flat R (↑H ⧸ Subalgebra.toSubmodule I.coinvariants)]`: the quotient module $H/B$, $H$ modulo the coinvariants viewed as an $R$-submodule, is flat over $R$.
- `(hI : I.IsNormal)`: $I$ is normal, $c(I) \subseteq H \otimes I$ for the coordinate map $c$ of conjugation: conjugation preserves $N$.
- The conclusion: a `Subcoalgebra R ↑H`, an $R$-submodule $D$ of $H$ with $\Delta(D)$ inside the image of $D \otimes_R D$ in $H \otimes_R H$.
- The value: `Subcoalgebra.ofSubmodule` applied to the coinvariants, so the carrier is $B = \{h : (\mathrm{id} \otimes \pi)(\Delta h) = h \otimes 1\}$ with $\pi : H \to H/I$ the quotient map. The proof puts $\Delta(h)$ in the image of $H \otimes B$ and, by normality, in that of $B \otimes H$; flatness of $H/B$ makes their intersection the image of $B \otimes B$.

On points: if $h(gn) = h(g)$ for $n$ in $N$, then $h(gg')$ is right $N$-invariant in $g'$, and, since $g'^{-1} n g'$ is in $N$, $h(gng') = h(gg')$, so it is right $N$-invariant in $g$ too. This is the standard step towards the quotient $G/N$, whose coordinate ring is $B$. Over a field both flatness hypotheses hold, as the docstring notes.

## References and tests
- [Milne, Definition 3.8](https://www.jmilne.org/math/Books/iAG2022.pdf#page=78) — the closure under comultiplication asked of $B$.
- `Submodule.range_map_subtype_subtype` — for submodules $P$ of $M$ and $Q$ of $N$ with $M/P$ flat, the image of $P \otimes Q$ in $M \otimes N$ is the intersection of the images of $M \otimes Q$ and $P \otimes N$.
- `TauCeti.HopfIdeal.IsNormal.mem_coinvariantsSubcoalgebra` — under the same hypotheses, the elements of the subcoalgebra are exactly the coinvariants.

The first test is the intersection formula the definition rests on, where the flatness of $H/B$ enters; the second checks that the carrier is $B$ itself.
